Imagine a smoke alarm. It can fail by staying silent during a real fire, which is terrible. Or, it can scream every time you make toast, which is very annoying! A good alarm finds the right balance. Binary classifiers, like those in machine learning, face similar trade-offs in their predictions.

Just like smoke alarms, machine learning models can make two kinds of mistakes. Accuracy alone can be misleading, especially for rare events like diseases. We'll learn to count these mistakes in a confusion matrix, then use precision, recall, and F1 score to truly understand how well a model performs.

Let's work through an example. Out of 500 patients, 110 are truly sick. Our model predicted 120 as sick, and 90 of those were correct. From this, we can calculate our true positives, false positives, false negatives, and true negatives, then precision, recall, and F1 score.

For your exams, always sketch the confusion matrix first! Remember scikit-learn's specific layout. Be careful with precision's (predicted positives) and recall's (actual positives) denominators. Accuracy often misleads on imbalanced data. Raising a threshold usually increases precision but lowers recall. You've learned crucial evaluation metrics this week!
